data.title: SIV Ambulances Enters Ambulance Manufacturing with Launch of SIV Responder and Responder XL Type II Ambulances
data.description:
SIV Ambulances Enters Ambulance Manufacturing with Launch of SIV Responder and Responder XL Type II Ambulances

SIV Ambulances has spent 2026 quietly building its Type II manufacturing program and is now introducing two Ford Transit Type II ambulances — the SIV Responder (Medium Roof) and SIV Responder XL (High Roof).

“This is a defining moment for SIV,” said Sergio Siv, CEO of SIV Ambulances. “We are the new generation. The decades-long era of the same names dominating this industry is over. We’re just getting started, and this is only the first move.”

NEW TO MANUFACTURING. NOT NEW TO AMBULANCES

SIV Ambulances has entered manufacturing with relationships built across the industry. EMS agencies nationwide and dealer partners have worked with SIV for years, establishing trust long before the launch of its own ambulance.

SIV has also completed more than 500 ambulance remounts. Hundreds of ambulances taken apart, rebuilt and returned to service gave the SIV team firsthand experience with how different designs, materials and systems perform over time — and a strong foundation to build from.

“High-quality remounting is one of the hardest things to do well in this industry,” Siv said. “Every ambulance is different. You’re dealing with different manufacturers, different electrical systems, discontinued components, parts that break during disassembly, new equipment that has to integrate with old systems, and customer changes throughout the process. You learn to solve problems every single day. Manufacturing feels easy to us because we started with the hard part first.”

That experience, combined with direct input from EMS agencies, helped shape the SIV Responder.

“We didn’t spend 2026 talking about becoming an ambulance manufacturer. We spent it building ambulances,” said Mark Poberezhnyuk, President of SIV’s Type II Division. “We built the team, developed the process and put the Responder into production. Now we’re ready to scale.”

$20 MILLION MANUFACTURING EXPANSION

SIV is backing its move into ambulance manufacturing with a $20 million expansion plan focused on growing its workforce, inventory, infrastructure and production capacity.

The plan includes a new purpose-built ambulance manufacturing facility in Pennsylvania, expanded chassis and parts inventory, additional manufacturing equipment and continued investment in SIV’s growing workforce. Architectural and civil engineering plans for the new facility are being finalized as SIV prepares to expand beyond its current manufacturing capacity.

The expansion will add significant capacity to SIV’s existing manufacturing operations creating new jobs and supporting the company’s continued growth in Pennsylvania.

“We’re putting $20 million behind the future of SIV,” Siv said. “We’re investing in people, inventory, production and a new manufacturing home. We’re building for the company we intend to become, not the company we are today. We know exactly where we’re going.”

About SIV Ambulances

SIV Ambulances is a Pennsylvania-based ambulance brand serving EMS agencies and dealer partners nationwide. SIV's operations include new ambulance manufacturing, ambulance remounting, new and used ambulance sales, service, parts, collision repair and fleet support. SIV has completed more than 500 ambulance remounts and is expanding its new ambulance manufacturing operations with the launch of the SIV Responder and Responder XL Type II ambulances.

data.title: USPS Salutes the U.S. Coast Guard Academy's 150 Years
data.description:
USPS Salutes the U.S. Coast Guard Academy's 150 Years

USPS Salutes the U.S. Coast Guard Academy's 150 Years

PR Newswire

NEW LONDON, Conn., Sept. 12, 2026

The stamp celebrates all the cadets whose dedication embodies the Coast Guard motto: Semper Paratus (Always Ready)

NEW LONDON, Conn., Sept. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Postal Service continues its tradition of honoring American military academies by issuing a stamp commemorating the 150th anniversary of the U.S. Coast Guard Academy. A dedication ceremony for the stamp was held today at Custom House Pier in New London.

"U.S. postage stamps celebrate the very best of America, and we are proud to feature the U.S. Coast Guard Academy on millions of letters that will be sent across the country," said Marc McCrery, USPS customer experience vice president and dedicating official. "I hope this stamp will serve as a reminder of how the cadets who graduate from the academy will serve with bravery and excellence and follow the Coast Guard motto: Semper Paratus — Always Ready." 

Joining McCrery were Rear Adm. Gregory C. Rothrock, U.S. Coast Guard Academy superintendent, and Capt. Kristopher Ensley, the USCGC Eagle training vessel's commanding officer.

The academy educates young cadets and provides them with the skills and experience they need to successfully lead others as officers in the U.S. Coast Guard. The academy develops leaders of character who will shape the future of the service as it transforms into a more agile, capable and responsive fighting force ready to meet the complex global challenges of the 21st century.

"We are incredibly proud that the Postal Service has chosen to honor the Coast Guard Academy with this stamp," said Rothrock said. "This recognition highlights the critical importance of the Coast Guard to our nation's security and our unwavering commitment to developing the next generation of Coast Guard officers."

The Academy's History

On July 31, 1876, Congress passed legislation authorizing what would become the U.S. Coast Guard Academy. Originally named the Revenue Cutter School of Instruction, it started with no real campus in the traditional sense.

Instead, on May 25, 1877, nine cadets joined three officers, a surgeon, six warrant officers and 17 enlisted crewmen for an extended training mission aboard the topsail schooner James C. Dobbin. This established a core principle that remains true today: The sea is the ultimate proving ground for a Coast Guard officer. Over the course of their journey, the cadets learned the foundational navigation and sailing skills that would prepare them for careers securing the nation's ports and waterways as officers in the Revenue Cutter Service.

The following year, a new three-masted barque — the cutter Salmon P. Chase — replaced the aging Dobbin. The Chase would go on to serve as the school's primary training vessel for nearly three decades, cementing a proud legacy that later training ships such as the Itasca and Eagle would carry into the future.

The Revenue Cutter School of Instruction moved ashore in 1900, first taking up residence in Curtis Bay, MD. In 1910, it moved to Fort Trumbull outside of New London. The school became known as the U.S. Coast Guard Academy after the merger of the Revenue Cutter Service and the Life Saving Service formed the Coast Guard in 1915. Additional maritime agencies combined with the organization over the years to form the Coast Guard of today. In 1932, the school outgrew the confines of Fort Trumbull and moved to a new campus two miles up the river. In the years since, it has grown to include more than 30 buildings across 103 acres. The academy began accepting women into its ranks in 1976.

Today, the academy boasts a student body of around 1,070 cadets. Applicants must meet high academic standards, display strong ethics and pass a physical fitness exam before earning a spot. Cadets can select one of 10 majors, including government, marine and environmental sciences, cyber systems, and several engineering disciplines. Additionally, like their predecessors aboard the Dobbin and the Chase, all cadets gain firsthand knowledge of seamanship aboard "America's Tall Ship," the barque Eagle, sometimes on weekslong cruises that carry them across oceans.

Each graduate commits to at least five years of service and earns both a Bachelor of Science degree and a commission as an ensign in the U.S. Coast Guard. Most elect to serve beyond their initial commitments. As officers, graduates take leadership roles among the Coast Guard's many essential missions, which include defending the nation, protecting the marine transportation system, regulating and safeguarding ports and waterways, maritime drug interdiction, and securing the maritime border.

Graduates will serve aboard the most technologically advanced vessels in Coast Guard history, providing key contributions demonstrating the Coast Guard's essential role in protecting our nation's interests at home and abroad. While the Coast Guard works primarily in and around U.S. waters, it also conducts international operations, including foreign port security inspections and polar icebreaking.

The Art of the Stamp

The stamp art features photographs of the barque Eagle, the academy's primary training vessel since 1946, and USCGC Bertholf, a Legend-class national security cutter whose missions include maritime drug interdiction and securing the maritime border.

Antonio Alcalá, an art director for USPS, designed this stamp. The Eagle photo was taken by Coast Guard Petty Officer 2nd Class Matthew Thieme and the Bertholf photo was taken by Coast Guard Petty Officer 1st Class Steven Strohmaier.

"Eagle is more than just a beautiful ship; it is a vital floating classroom where cadets forge the leadership and seamanship skills required to lead in today's Coast Guard," Ensley said. "We deeply appreciate Eagle being featured on this stamp, honoring the rigorous training that ensures our service remains always ready."

The stamps come in panes of 20. As Forever stamps, they will always be equal in value to the current First-Class Mail 1‑ounce price. News of the stamp is being shared with the hashtag #USCoastGuardStamp.

Postal Products

Customers may purchase stamps and other philatelic products through The Postal Store at usps.com/shopstamps, by calling 844-737-7826, by mail through USA Philatelic, or at Post Office locations nationwide. For officially licensed stamp products, shop the USPS Officially Licensed Collection on Amazon. Additional information on stamps, first-day-of-issue ceremonies and stamp-inspired products can be found at stampsforever.com.

Please Note: The United States Postal Service is an independent federal establishment, mandated to be self-financing and to serve every American community through the affordable, reliable and secure delivery of mail and packages to more than 170 million addresses six and often seven days a week. Overseen by a bipartisan Board of Governors, the Postal Service is currently pursuing a transformation plan aimed at restoring long-term financial sustainability, improving service, and maintaining the organization as one of America's most valued and trusted brands.

The Postal Service generally receives no tax dollars for operating expenses and relies on the sale of postage, products and services to fund its operations.

For USPS media resources, including broadcast-quality video and audio and photo stills, visit the USPS Newsroom. Follow us on X, Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Threads, and LinkedIn. Subscribe to the USPS YouTube Channel. For more information about the Postal Service, visit usps.com and facts.usps.com.

data.title: My 87-year-old mother wants to pay for my brother's kids' education. I don't have children. How is that fair?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'Over the years, my mother and I have supplemented his income'

"The understanding is that whatever she gives him would be deducted from his share of her estate after she dies." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

My 87-year-old mother recently asked whether I would be comfortable with her giving my younger brother part of his inheritance while she is still alive. The understanding is that whatever she gives him would be deducted from his share of her estate after she dies.

She would limit the money to educational expenses for his two children - one in college and one in middle school - and plans to pay the schools directly on his behalf. I'm not completely opposed to the idea, but I'm struggling with whether it's fair.

I have a higher-paying career, no biological children, and I'm married. My brother is 57, and I'm 60. I'm wondering whether I should suggest that my mother establish a trust or some other structured arrangement for these educational expenses rather than giving my brother money.

There is another concern behind my hesitation: My brother previously had corporate jobs earning six figures but left that career and now works at a job he enjoys that pays less than $50,000 a year. He has no interest in changing jobs or taking on a second job.

He has limited retirement savings and, despite having a business degree, has historically made some poor financial decisions. I do his taxes and occasionally help him with financial issues. Over the years, my mother and I have supplemented his income.

He lives fairly simply in some respects, but I'm concerned that if he receives a substantial amount of money outright, he may not manage it well. I also worry that, given his limited retirement savings and income, I may eventually be the person who has to support him.

So I'm trying to balance several things: honoring my mother's wishes, treating my brother fairly, protecting his children's educational opportunities, and not creating an expectation that I will ultimately be responsible for supporting my brother.

Should I encourage my mother to establish a trust or another structured arrangement for the educational expenses? Would it be reasonable for me to ask that an equivalent amount be given to me at the same time, even though I don't have children?

Worried Big Sister

Don't miss: 'I want safe returns': I'm 73 with $300,000 saved. I'm not interested in the stock market. What should I do?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Say "yes" to your mother's request, but don't make your blessing contingent on you getting the same amount.

Dear Big Sister,

This request has raised a lot of issues for you.

On the face of it, your mother's request is reasonable: set up a trust for her grandchildren so they can get support if/when they choose to attend university. This is a common and natural wish, especially given what you say about your brother's mismanagement of money.

Another natural response would be, "How would you feel about giving me the same amount so I can invest it in the stock market and to help my business grow?" Your mother may or may not agree to this. Your brother's kids need a leg-up in life. You, presumably, do not.

So this is my take: Say "yes" to your mother's request, but don't make your blessing - it is only a blessing, not permission, after all - contingent on you getting the same amount. That puts your mother under too much pressure. She's trying to do a good thing. Let her do it.

And if she says "no" to your request, take it on the chin like the good adult you are. You are the one who stuck to her original career plan, built her own future independently, did not give up a six-figure job to follow your heart or ask family members for handouts or loans.

I see why you are mixing your mother's wishes with your feelings about your brother. He's not always been the most fiscally responsible member of your family, and you fear that giving him a lump sum may end up in his pocket, rather than going towards the education of his kids.

But while your brother's lack of money management appears to have led your mother to make this gesture, it's also important not to punish his children for the sins of their father. The money, once set up in a trust, will go towards their education expenses. It's a clear path.

So what does your mother choose? A 529 tax-advantaged account or a trust? In this case, I favor a 529 plan. The biggest reason: a 529 plan is a state-sponsored college tuition account, so your mother's gift won't count against her grandchildren when applying for financial aid.

Related: My 5-year-old granddaughter says, 'Who's nana?' Should I set up a college trust fund for a child who does not even know who I am?

529 plan vs. trust

A 529 plan is generally a more tax-efficient option than a trust if your mother's primary goal is to save for her grandchildren's education. The earnings grow tax-free, and withdrawals are tax-free when used for qualified education expenses, like tuition, books, and room and board.

A trust would be more suitable if the money were for things other than education. Your mother would not be restricted by the terms of the 529 plan, which comes with a 10% penalty and ordinary income tax if the funds are withdrawn for something other than educational expenses.

Another advantage to a trust: For the most part, an irrevocable trust would shield assets from your mother's creditors, if she had any. (It does not sound like your grandmother is in bad financial shape, so that would likely not be a consideration in this case.)

What's more, a trust offers greater flexibility, but that freedom comes at a cost. Establishing and administering a trust can involve significant legal, accounting and administrative expenses, and any investment income from that trust may be subject to high federal income-tax rates.

That said, 529 plans are generous. In 2026, your mother can contribute up to $95,000 in one go by electing to front-load five years of annual gift-tax exclusions. (A married couple can contribute up to $190,000 in 2026, if all the requirements are met.)

Subject to rules, up to $35,000 of a 529 plan can be rolled into a Roth IRA for the beneficiary under Secure Act 2.0. Given that there are two beneficiaries, each could get that rollover amount. Your mother can read more about those terms and conditions here.

One more missing piece of this puzzle: Don't discount the pleasure your mother would get from being able to fund her grandchildren's education during her lifetime, and seeing them thrive, knowing that she had a hand in that. For her, that might be priceless.

Related: 'This is a first-world problem': I can't roll over my $800,000 401(k) from my prior employer. What did I do wrong?

data.title: HVAC Expert Darrin Monks Explains How Dry Air Impacts Indoor Air Quality and Health in Colorado Homes in HelloNation
data.description:
HVAC Expert Darrin Monks Explains How Dry Air Impacts Indoor Air Quality and Health in Colorado Homes in HelloNation

HVAC Expert Darrin Monks Explains How Dry Air Impacts Indoor Air Quality and Health in Colorado Homes in HelloNation

PR Newswire

STRASBURG, Colo., Sept. 12, 2026

The article outlines how humidity control and proper HVAC planning support comfort, efficiency, and healthier indoor environments.

STRASBURG, Colo., Sept. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- How does dry Colorado air affect indoor air quality and overall health inside the home? HelloNation has published the answer in an article featuring insights from HVAC Expert Darrin Monks of U.S. Mechanical Company in Strasburg, Colorado.

The HelloNation article explains that indoor air quality is a critical but often overlooked part of home comfort. In Strasburg, Colorado, dry air is common, especially during the winter months. The article notes that low humidity levels can irritate the eyes, nose, and throat and may worsen asthma or allergy symptoms.

According to the article, dry air also affects more than personal comfort. It can increase static electricity and cause damage to wood floors, furniture, and musical instruments. Addressing indoor air quality in Strasburg, CO, helps protect both health and household materials throughout the year.

The article describes how the region's high elevation, cold winters, and naturally low humidity create ongoing challenges. When heating systems run during colder months, they can further reduce indoor moisture levels. This combination often leaves homes feeling colder and less comfortable, even when thermostats are set at normal temperatures.

Managing humidity properly can improve both comfort and HVAC performance. The article explains that many homeowners begin with portable units, but these often provide uneven coverage. A whole-home humidifier offers a more consistent solution by distributing moisture evenly through the HVAC system.

Dry air can also affect equipment efficiency. The article notes that when humidity levels are too low, heating systems may work harder to maintain comfort. This added strain can increase energy use and lead to more frequent HVAC repairs. Integrating a whole-home humidifier with an energy-efficient HVAC setup can reduce wear and support more stable indoor temperatures.

The HelloNation article also highlights the benefits of pairing humidity control with smart thermostat installation in Strasburg. This combination allows homeowners to monitor and adjust both temperature and moisture levels more precisely. Improved control can enhance comfort while supporting lower monthly utility costs.

Beyond dryness, the article addresses airborne particles such as dust and pollen that can accumulate when homes remain closed during winter. Regular HVAC maintenance, including filter replacement and duct cleaning, plays an important role in protecting indoor air quality. A properly maintained HVAC system combined with humidifier installation can promote cleaner air and healthier breathing conditions.

The article emphasizes that children, seniors, and individuals with respiratory concerns may be especially sensitive to poor indoor air quality. Common symptoms of dry air include itchy eyes, sore throats, dry skin, and persistent coughing. Balanced humidity levels can ease these symptoms and create a more supportive indoor environment.

Professional planning is another key theme. The article explains that humidifier installation should be coordinated with properly sized equipment to ensure even air distribution. HVAC installation in Strasburg, CO, performed by experienced contractors helps ensure that all components work together efficiently and reduces the likelihood of future HVAC repair.

Cost considerations are also addressed. While installing a whole-home humidifier or upgrading to an energy-efficient HVAC system requires upfront investment, the article notes that long-term benefits often include fewer repairs, improved comfort, and lower energy bills. Careful equipment selection and qualified installation support lasting results.

The article concludes that improving indoor air quality through humidity control, routine maintenance, and thoughtful HVAC system design directly supports health and comfort. In Colorado's dry climate, proactive solutions help homeowners maintain balanced air, protect their homes, and promote well-being year-round.

Understanding Indoor Air Quality: Why Dry Colorado Air Impacts Your Health features insights from Darrin Monks, HVAC Expert of Strasburg, Colorado, in HelloNation.

data.title: Endodontist Expert Dr. Christopher Joubert Explains What Endodontic Care Is and How It Protects Natural Teeth in HelloNation
data.description:
Endodontist Expert Dr. Christopher Joubert Explains What Endodontic Care Is and How It Protects Natural Teeth in HelloNation

Endodontist Expert Dr. Christopher Joubert Explains What Endodontic Care Is and How It Protects Natural Teeth in HelloNation

PR Newswire

PATCHOGUE, N.Y., Sept. 12, 2026

The article details how endodontic care treats inner tooth problems and prevents long-term damage from tooth infection.

PATCHOGUE, N.Y., Sept. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What is endodontic care, and why is it essential for treating inner tooth problems? That question is answered in a HelloNation article that features insights from Dr. Christopher Joubert of East Endodontic Dental Specialists in Patchogue, New York.

The HelloNation article explains that endodontic care focuses on diagnosing and treating problems inside the tooth, especially issues involving the pulp and nerves. According to the article, these conditions often stem from tooth infection, deep decay, cracks, dental trauma, or failed previous treatments. The article notes that an untreated tooth infection can spread into bone and soft tissue, potentially causing abscesses and long-term damage. The primary goal of endodontic care is to save the natural tooth whenever possible while restoring health and long-term tooth stability.

The article describes how tooth infection rarely improves without proper treatment. When bacteria reach the pulp, they multiply and may spread into surrounding structures. The article explains that this can lead to swelling, pain, and more advanced complications, including effects on nearby teeth and overall oral wellness. Early endodontic care helps control infection, relieve pain, and increase the chance of saving the natural tooth before additional problems develop.

Root canal therapy is described as the most common dental procedure within endodontic care. The HelloNation article outlines each step of this dental procedure, including removing infected pulp, cleaning and shaping the canals, disinfecting the internal space, and sealing the tooth with a durable material to prevent reinfection. A final dental restoration, such as a crown or filling, strengthens the tooth and restores function. The article explains that modern techniques, including 3D imaging and operating microscopes, help locate hidden canals or fractures that may otherwise be missed, improving the overall success of the treatment.

Endodontic care also plays a key role in treating cracked or injured teeth. The article explains that early evaluation can prevent infection from spreading deeper and causing bone loss. Preserving the natural tooth supports proper bite alignment and helps maintain jawbone health. The article notes that extracted teeth, even when replaced with implants or bridges, may not preserve the bone or alignment as effectively as natural teeth. Maintaining natural teeth also reduces stress on neighboring teeth and avoids shifting or uneven wear.

According to the article, successful endodontic care depends on accurate diagnosis, precise technique, and proper restoration. A high-quality dental restoration protects the tooth after treatment and helps it function normally for many years. Routine dental checkups and strong oral hygiene habits support long-term tooth health and reduce the risk of reinfection. Brushing and flossing daily helps ensure that endodontic treatment results are preserved.

The article highlights that modern endodontic care is generally comfortable for patients. Local anesthesia and advanced instruments help reduce discomfort during treatment. Most patients experience only mild soreness afterward, which usually resolves within a few days. Because endodontists specialize in treating complex cases, they can manage situations involving unusual canal anatomy, previous failed procedures, or significant dental trauma. The article emphasizes that specialized training and advanced tools help increase success rates and improve outcomes.

Neglecting a tooth infection can have serious consequences. The article explains that untreated infections may spread to nearby teeth, damage surrounding bone, or contribute to broader health concerns. Early endodontic care helps prevent these problems, preserves the natural tooth, and supports overall tooth health. Patients benefit from maintaining normal chewing and speaking function while protecting long-term oral wellness.

The article concludes that endodontic care is an essential part of preserving natural teeth and maintaining strong oral health. Through careful diagnosis, precise treatment, and consistent follow-up, endodontists can save teeth that might otherwise be lost to infection, trauma, or decay. Proper endodontic treatment is described as a reliable and proven way to protect natural teeth and maintain long-term dental stability.

By Quentin Fottrell

"I would arrange everything privately, in coordination only with the management and staff of each restaurant." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I lost my beloved husband earlier this year after a long illness. I miss him profoundly. His passing was not unexpected, but honoring his simple, decent memory is very important to me in the days and years ahead.

My husband enjoyed humble pleasures, and he had two favorite fast-casual restaurants where the food was good, the patrons were kind, and the staff were simply salt-of-the-earth people. With that in mind, I have an idea for a small tribute to him.

In 2027, on his birthday in April and in September, on the anniversary of our first date, I would like to pay for every order placed by walk-in customers - from open to close - at each of these two restaurants.

No online orders, and no fanfare or publicity. I would arrange everything privately, in coordination only with the management and staff of each restaurant. I've researched the revenues of both locations and can comfortably afford to do this.

My husband enjoyed humble pleasures, and he had two favorite fast-casual restaurants where the food was good.

It would be my own little way of honoring my husband: supporting two local businesses he loved and, for one day, treating the people who patronize them with the same simple generosity and kindness that characterized him.

My question is: How would I best arrange the logistics with each restaurant, and what would be the most reliable way to handle payment? I could certainly put the charges on my credit cards as customers came through.

However, I'm concerned that my card issuers might freeze or flag the cards when they suddenly see an extraordinary number of transactions. I could also put down a substantial good-faith deposit and settle the balance at the end of the day if the total exceeds the deposit.

Beyond those possibilities, though, I'm completely stumped. I'd love to hear any practical suggestions for structuring this so that it is easy for the restaurant, seamless for the staff and customers, and doesn't create unnecessary headaches for anyone.

A Kind Remembrance

Related: 'This guy grifted me hard': My date chose an exclusive L.A. restaurant. After dinner, he accepted my credit card - and we split a $600 bill. Shouldn't he have paid?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

You would be relying on the restaurant management not to spill the beans to regular customers and employees.

Dear Kind,

Your idea is pretty special, but perhaps needs a little finessing.

My main piece of advice would be for you to put a lid - excuse the pun - on how much you spend. If you get an estimate from each restaurant that they do, say, $10,000 worth of business that day, you could make sure that the day's transactions do not exceed that.

There are a lot of questions that would need answering: Does your generosity include sales tax and tips? What happens if somebody orders $500 worth of food for a group or $500 worth of booze, and you suspect they got wind of your charitable endeavor? Do you want to cover tips?

You would also be relying on the restaurant management not to spill the beans - apologies once again for the pun - to regular customers and employees. You could have customers showing up ordering a feast of fillet steaks because they got an inside tip on your generosity.

For that reason, consider matching receipts rather than giving your credit cards to employees. Too much could go wrong. Also, think about whether you want to cover alcoholic drinks. If word got around, a lot of Dom Perignon might miraculously be in demand that day.

By paying the customer's bills, they get to have a free meal, but the restaurant still gets paid for the day's receipts.

Ideally, I'd like you to balance the emotion and romance and beauty of your generosity with the practicality of implementing it, while taking the peculiar habits of human beings into account (chief among them, people love a bargain, and news of a $0 meal will spread like wildfire).

Perhaps tell the restaurant management something along the lines of: "I would like to cover the cost of every walk-in customer's food and soft drink, anonymously and without publicity. I want your staff to operate exactly as usual. I will match their bills."

But don't be surprised if the unusual event ends up in the local paper. You can control very few things in this life, and word-of-mouth news is chief among them. You may decide to do a trial run for your late husband's birthday and maybe try something different for your anniversary.

One more thought: By paying the customer's bills, they get to have a free meal, but the restaurant still gets paid for the day's receipts. If these restaurants are owned by a giant global conglomerate, you're also giving that money to that company.

Related: 'We fear financial exploitation': Who will manage our finances if my wife and I become incapacitated?

Remembering the staff

I also wonder whether it would mean more to direct your largesse towards the wait and kitchen staff rather than random customers. Sure, each person might find their $25 lunch has been picked up by a mysterious benefactor. That customer might be a multimillionaire.

And even if your gesture doesn't have a big financial impact on each customer, I'm sure the small act of kindness would be gratefully received by each customer you comp on that day. Again, be prepared that they may spread the word about the $0 meals. Good news travels fast.

You could arguably make a bigger impact by matching the day's receipts and giving that money to the employees, even those who were not working on that particular day (as long as management doesn't pocket it). There are just so many ways to peel this onion.

Members of the Moneyist Facebook Group also suggest remembering the staff in your 24-hour bonanza at these two establishments. One woman writes: "I like the idea of honoring the staff. If you were to pick up my $100 tab, I'd like it, sure."

You could, arguably, make a bigger impact by matching the day's receipts and giving that money to the employees.

"But if each staff member got $100," she adds, "that money would go directly to the people who made these spots special. It would go to buy school supplies, pay a light bill, or fund dinner out for someone who might otherwise not afford it."

Another Moneyist Facebook Group (META) member said that she did something similar to what you are planning. "I did this at a Chick-fil-A in Santa Rosa after fires burned down part of the town some years ago. I didn't prearrange it so that might make a difference."

"I had collected money from friends so it wasn't all me. Anyways, Chick-fil-A needed to use my physical credit card to ring up each individual order. The manager would periodically check with me to see if the total was okay. I believe I did have to switch credit cards after a while."

"People were so grateful as everyone in the area was so stressed out," she adds. "I actually sat with a group who were dining in and we chatted for a while. What you want to do is great but if you think so highly of the staff, maybe you should do something for them, too."

Whatever you decide, your husband would be proud.

data.title: New Delhi Marks UN Day for South-South Cooperation with Push to Scale Dryland Innovation Across the Global South
data.description:
New Delhi Marks UN Day for South-South Cooperation with Push to Scale Dryland Innovation Across the Global South

New Delhi Marks UN Day for South-South Cooperation with Push to Scale Dryland Innovation Across the Global South

PR Newswire

NEW DELHI, Sept. 12, 2026

NEW DELHI, Sept. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A major international push to accelerate agricultural innovation across the Global South took centre stage in New Delhi today, as the United Nations Day for South-South Cooperation was commemorated amid mounting climate, water and food-security pressures across the world's drylands.

Held as part of the Global Drylands Congress 2026, the commemoration focused on how proven solutions can move faster across borders, particularly between countries facing similar agricultural and climate conditions, be adapted to local realities and deliver greater impact for farmers and food systems.

The Congress brought together some of the world's foremost agricultural scientists, policymakers, research leaders, development institutions, private-sector actors and practitioners, creating a high-level global platform to help shape the future of dryland agriculture and strengthen cooperation across the Global South.

The commemoration showcased the growing reach of the ICRISAT Centre of Excellence for South-South Cooperation in Agriculture (ISSCA), a global platform accelerating the adaptation and scaling of proven agricultural solutions across the Global South.

ISSCA now works with 19 partners, has identified more than 100 validated and scalable solutions, and has supported over 300 professionals from more than 40 countries. Its portfolio spans climate-resilient crops, soil and water management, digital agriculture, agribusiness, nutrition, livelihoods and environmental sustainability.

That approach carries particular urgency for the world's drylands, home to hundreds of millions of people and among the regions most exposed to climate variability, water scarcity, land degradation and food insecurity. Yet these same regions are also emerging as important frontiers for innovation in climate-resilient agriculture.

The Dryland Congress was jointly organized by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) and the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT), bringing together two globally renowned agricultural research institutions with a long history of collaboration in crop improvement, resilient farming systems, natural resource management and dryland innovation.

ICAR, one of the world's largest national agricultural research systems, has played a central role in India's agricultural transformation, drawing on deep scientific expertise, institutional strength and experience at scale. ICRISAT, a CGIAR Research Center, brings more than five decades of scientific leadership across the drylands of Asia and Africa, with a distinguished record of advancing crop improvement, farming systems and natural resource management, while translating research into practical solutions for food and nutrition security and livelihoods.

Addressing the Congress, ICRISAT Director General Dr Himanshu Pathak said ISSCA's growth reflected a broader evolution in South-South cooperation — moving beyond knowledge exchange towards practical pathways for adoption and impact.

"Rather than reinventing solutions country by country, ISSCA connects proven innovations with institutions, partners and farming systems where they can be adapted and scaled more rapidly.

"The Global Drylands Congress has strengthened that pathway by bringing together science, policy, partnerships and investment to turn proven solutions into impact at scale," Dr Pathak said.

Dr M.L. Jat, Secretary, DARE and Director General, ICAR, underscored that the future of agriculture will increasingly depend on countries and institutions working together across borders.

"It will be shaped by what we are willing to share, what we can learn from one another, and how boldly we build partnerships that turn science into solutions for farmers.

"The ICAR–ICRISAT partnership is a powerful example of what sustained collaboration can achieve, and of the wider promise of South-South cooperation," Dr Jat said.

The commemoration culminated in the presentation of the Delhi Declaration on Drylands, setting out a shared ambition to strengthen South-South cooperation, accelerate the uptake and scaling of proven innovations, deepen institutional partnerships and reposition the world's drylands as landscapes of resilience, opportunity and sustainable growth.

data.title: 'I still don't have my MRI': My health insurer canceled my plan without warning. Is that legal?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'It wasn't an ACA plan, but it was meaningfully cheaper than anything I could find on the ACA exchange"

"It was marketed as group coverage for self-employed 'working owners,' and it was meaningfully cheaper than anything I could find on the ACA exchange." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I've spent 40 years working in IT. I know how to verify a system, troubleshoot a failure and stay calm when something breaks. None of that helped me on the Tuesday after Labor Day, when a billing representative told me - after an hour on hold - that the health insurance I'd been paying for through my LLC no longer technically existed.

I'm self-employed, running a small consulting business through my own LLC. Like a lot of self-employed people, every year I run the numbers and find that an Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace plan at the full, unsubsidized price is more expensive than one of the "alternative" group plans marketed to freelancers and gig workers. I chose the latter, a PPO plan.

It wasn't an ACA plan, but it was meaningfully cheaper than anything I could find on the ACA exchange. It worked fine - until I actually needed it. I was trying to schedule a hip MRI on both hips when the imaging center told me my coverage was "not active." I was told its verification system was simply down. Fair enough. Systems go down. After 40 years in IT, I get it.

But when the imaging center called back, my coverage was still showing as inactive. This time, after another hour on hold, I got a real answer: Effective Sept. 1, the Nebraska insurance company dropped my policies entirely - the entire group - and the third-party administrator was "in the process" of moving affected members to another "ACME" insurer.

It wasn't an ACA plan, but it was meaningfully cheaper than anything I could find on the ACA exchange.

There had been no advance notice. No letter. No email. Just the explanation that the verification system was down - an explanation that, in hindsight, seems to have concealed the more important fact that my coverage had already ended three days earlier. I still don't have my MRI, and I don't yet know whether the doctor who ordered it even accepts the ACME insurer.

That's where I'm stuck, and where I'm hoping you can help: Is there any meaningful recourse against an administrator that provides essentially no notice before a network termination like this? Is there a regulator or complaint process that actually has teeth, rather than simply generating a case number?

It feels as though I did everything a reasonably careful consumer could do. Is the loss of non-ACA "Working Owner" coverage like this ever considered a qualifying life event for an ACA Marketplace Special Enrollment Period? Or does the fact that this wasn't ACA coverage in the first place shut that door?

For the immediate problem - an MRI I need, with my insurance coverage in limbo - is there a smarter move than either paying cash or waiting for an insurer? And for the future, are there self-employed coverage options I've overlooked that don't carry this kind of tail risk, short of simply going back to a full-price ACA plan?

Self-Employed and Stuck

Related: 'I'm not interested in long-term care insurance': I'd like to retire at 55. How much will I have to pay for healthcare?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

A health-insurance company cannot terminate your coverage without 30 days of advance written notice.

Dear Self-Employed,

Either they dropped the ball, or you missed the letter.

Fully insured, state-regulated plans require insurers to give you written notice before terminating coverage - usually 30 or 60 days. Unless you actually set out to defraud the insurer, the company may not cancel your coverage even if you made a mistake on your application. But you do need to determine what law governs your plan - the Affordable Care Act of 2010 (ACA) and/or Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA).

Whether or not losing your coverage opens a Marketplace Special Enrollment Period (SEP) largely depends on whether your insurance contains "minimum essential coverage" (MEC). Many "alternative" or association-style plans sold to the self-employed do not have MEC, which is why they are often cheaper than ACA plans. If your plan was sold to you as "working owner" coverage, it's governed by the Employee Retirement Income Security Act.

A lower premium isn't necessarily the bargain if the end of the policy leaves you with a gap in your coverage.

To eliminate "tail risk," the catastrophic exposure of an uncapped medical emergency, use coverage that falls under ACA's consumer protections, as outlined in Healthcare.gov's guide to what ACA plans cover. Open Enrollment is between Nov. 1 and Jan. 15. If you enroll by Dec. 15, coverage begins Jan. 1. If you enroll between Dec. 16 and Jan. 15, coverage starts Feb. 1. Unfortunately, that's four to five months from now, but it's still worth pursuing.

As for your MRI: ask the doctor who ordered it whether the imaging is time-sensitive, and weigh the risk of delay. Separately, call the imaging center directly and ask about a self-pay or prompt-pay rate, which can be a fraction of billed charges - and ask your third-party administrator whether your "ACME" coverage will be retroactive to Sept. 1. Ask them, in writing, for evidence that they gave you the required notice, and why the coverage was dropped.

Don't miss: 'It feels like a medical miracle': How did a single QR code coupon cut my $618 Walgreens prescription to $15?

Alleged lack of notice

The National Association of Insurance Commissioners should direct you to the insurance commissioner in your state. But first, determine whether you had state-regulated insurance. If the arrangement is self-funded or otherwise subject to the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), the state insurance department may have limited jurisdiction. If that's the case, contact the Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration instead.

Regarding the alleged lack of notice, you can compile the evidence - emails and screenshots - from your insurance company, and put your case to them in writing that you were, as you suggest, unceremoniously dropped without notice, and "cc" your broker or the association that sponsored your plan. Keep original documents, certificates of coverage, premium records, small print relating to your benefits, and reference numbers of all communications/complaints.

Finally, before buying another "alternative" plan to the ACA marketplace, find out exactly what you're buying, whether the plan is fully insured or self-funded, subject to state insurance regulation or subject to ACA requirements and, crucially, what happens if the sponsoring group or insurer disappears again. A lower premium isn't the bargain it appears to be if the policy's cancellation leaves you with this kind of uncertainty and, worse, a gap in your coverage.

Good luck with this bureaucracy of becoming unstuck.
